值得閱讀的理由

  • 深刻剖析中共政權在經歷大飢荒、文革及六四等重大災難後，為何未如蘇聯或東歐劇變般瓦解的根本歷史機制。
  • 打破「改革開放是中共存活唯一原因」的單一迷思，揭示鄧小平轉向背後早已建構完成的強大國家機器與社會控制基礎。
  • 比較國民黨與共產黨不同的建國路徑，闡述中共如何透過革命戰爭消除地方勢力、消滅民間組織，將社會原子化以防堵政權崩潰。

摘要

政權生存的世紀之謎與改革開放的前提

作者探討了一個鮮少有人認真回答的深層政治問題：一個造成數千萬人飢荒、瀕臨內戰邊緣，甚至在首都向人民開槍的政權，為何沒有在1960年、1976年或1989年崩潰，反而在當代成為世界第二大經濟體？外界多將其歸功於鄧小平的改革開放與經濟奇蹟，然而作者指出，真正的關鍵在於1978年鄧小平能夠瞬間調頭、徹底推翻毛澤東數十年的階級鬥爭路線，卻未遭遇任何地方分裂、軍事叛變或組織性抗爭。這意味著在改革開放之前，這套高度集權的極權國家機器就已經建造完成，改革開放僅是啟動機器的結果，而非故事的起點。

革命政權的獨特韌性與三大遺產

從清朝覆滅到軍閥割據，近代中國長期處於權力碎片化狀態，最終卻催生了史上最具韌性的威權體制之一。作者引用學術研究指出，由漫長且殘酷的社會革命所誕生的政權（如中、蘇、古巴、越南），往往對經濟危機、政策災難與外部制裁展現出極強的免疫力。這場革命留下了三項關鍵資產：以生死紐帶緊密結合的統治菁英階層、完全效忠該群體的暴力暴力專政機器，以及徹底被原子化、失去組織能力的社會。一般威權政權崩潰的三大途徑——菁英分裂、軍事政變與大眾起義，在早期暴力革命的淬鍊下已被完全封堵。

國共建國路徑之別與極權組織的成型

相較於國民黨採取懷柔與收編軍閥、鄉紳以求快速統戰，卻留下各自為政的後患；中共選擇以暴力手段徹底剷除地主階級與地方軍閥，將權力徹底滲透至農村、工廠與家庭餐桌。歷經1927年清黨的重創後，毛澤東確立了「槍桿子裡面出政權」的原則，打造了黨軍一體的架構。隨後的長征更成為極權體制凝聚的轉捩點，在經歷殘酷淘汰後，留下了極為精簡且忠誠的領導核心，不僅確立了毛澤東的絕對權力，更鍛造出國民黨派系所無法比擬的深厚信任與高度凝聚力，成為日後政權維繫數十年的最核心政治資產。

================================================

Ten years after this regime starved tens of millions of its own people, it pushed the country to the brink of full-scale civil war, and twenty years after that, it opened fire on its own people in its own capital. For a regime to reach this level, by any standard of political common sense, it should have been gone long ago. Yet, it never once collapsed; not only did it survive, but it also grew into the world's second-largest economy over the past few decades. The Soviet Union, its contemporary, collapsed; the socialist bloc in Eastern Europe, from Poland to Romania, fell like dominoes within two years. Even its neighbor across the strait, Taiwan, and. its neighbor to the northeast, South Korea, ended their authoritarian rule in the late 1980s and embraced liberal democracy. Yet, the one-party Chinese Communist Party has remained in power in China to this day. I have produced many episodes arguing that the CCP's rule has entered a countdown. Today, I want to answer a different question—a harder one that few are willing to answer seriously : Why didn't this countdown happen in 1960, 1976, or 1989? How has a regime that has committed every possible mistake survived until today? I know. many will say Deng Xiaoping's "Reform and Opening-up" saved the CCP. This has been the prevailing view in Western academia and politics for the past 40 years: economic growth bought social stability, and the CCP stayed stable because it knew how to adapt and was lucky enough to catch the global takeoff of the 80s and 90s. The scale of China’s economic transformation is indeed astonishing—no one can deny that—but by focusing only on these last 40 years, you miss an earlier and more important precondition: When Deng issued his order in 1978, he was able to overturn the entire line of class struggle that Mao. had pursued for decades. How was he able to do that? There was no organized resistance across the country, no provincial secession, no military mutiny , and no political faction stood up to say no. How could he achieve this? The answer is that before he issued his order, someone had already built this country for him. A machine that would turn as a whole as soon as Zhongnanhai flipped the switch. The Reform and Opening-up was the result of this machine starting, but it was not the beginning of the story. Hello everyone, at the beginning of this episode, I’d like to take a moment to share a few personal thoughts. I’ve been making. these programs for seven years now, with over 2,000 episodes, and many viewers often ask: How do you acquire knowledge and information, and how do you analyze and judge them? So, the answer is finally revealed today in my latest book , "The Truth About 'Ru-Hua': Misunderstandings Between China and the World Order." This book covers everything from China's ancient and modern history to the history of the PRC , cross-strait issues, international relations, America's role in this order , and the underlying logic behind these current events. I believe this book is a massive resource for my friends in Taiwan and across the globe who embrace universal values and aim to be global citizens—it is a weapon for.

understanding the world and confronting authoritarianism. I consider this very important; it is the culmination of my work over the years, detailing my sources of knowledge, my analytical frameworks, and the process by which I reach my conclusions. It presents all of that, as many who have watched my " Gongzi Reads" series—which is currently on hiatus on my channel—can attest. All the content from that series is in this book, along with many new, even more significant theories and facts. Of course, I am standing on the shoulders of giants, utilizing a wealth of geopolitical and international relations. theories to enrich this book, providing better tools to understand world changes and our place in it, so we can live more harmoniously with this world. I hope you enjoy the book; it is now officially available for order on Books.com.tw in Taiwan. For those outside of Taiwan and its surrounding regions, such as in North America or Europe, I will announce other channels for purchase soon. Also, if you buy the book and would like it signed, there will be a book signing event in Taipei on December 5th; everyone is welcome, and I will post the time and address on my YouTube channel. Thank you, and now back to the main. topic. >> So first, we must return to history to find the answers. In 1911, the Qing Empire collapsed, and 2,000 years of imperial autocracy vanished overnight; over the next 30 years, warlords, secret societies, and local elites carved up the former Qing territories. From a chaotic, fragmented mess where factions constantly warred, one of the most enduring authoritarian regimes in modern history eventually emerged. This phenomenon demands an explanation, and the answer lies within the half-century-long Communist revolution. From 1925 to 1976, relying on Soviet support and successive waves of violent campaigns, the CCP forged a powerful, loyal force and a highly cohesive power core. This ultimately birthed the People's Republic of China, a party-state with integrated party, government, and military structures, clearing the way for decades of authoritarian rule. According to research from Harvard and the University of Toronto, if you compare regimes born from social revolutions—such as those in China, the USSR, Cuba, Iran, and Vietnam. —you find a common, exceptionally resilient trait: they are seemingly immune to economic crises, policy disasters, mass grievances, and external sanctions. What exactly is the reason for this? The reason lies in a revolutionary war that was sufficiently long and bloody, leaving them three precious legacies: a ruling elite bound by life-and-death ties, a violence-capable apparatus loyal solely to this group, and a hollowed-out, atomized society. Because all organizations capable of becoming competitors—churches, temples, military.

units, landed gentry, and chambers of commerce—were completely wiped out during the long process of so-called revolutionary struggle. Authoritarian regimes generally fall through only three paths: elite fragmentation, military coups, or mass uprisings; that Communist revolution happened to block all three. In the early 20th century, China was a tug-of-war between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party. They shared common enemies—imperialism, warlords, and local elites—all of which both parties verbally vowed to overthrow . However, when it came to the question of what kind of state to build, their. ideas were worlds apart. The Kuomintang's path was to integrate the existing warlords and have the landed gentry pledge loyalty to the Republic, trading the fastest unification for the lowest cost. This path looked smart, but the price was that those incorporated local forces never gave up their guns, their land, or their clan networks. Chiang Kai-shek unified China in name, but in reality, he held onto a group of partners who could turn against him at any moment. Mao Zedong and the Communist Party took a different path: they sought to eliminate the entire class of landlords who owned private property and. to uproot the warlords who defended local interests. The ultimate result of these nearly constant revolutionary movements was to force a nation with extremely fragmented power into a regime with highly centralized authority. For the first time in history, the so-called revolutionary struggle reached every village, every factory, every community , and even every household's dinner table in China. Initially, the Communist Party followed the Soviet model, pinning its hopes on the urban working class. That changed in April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek suddenly turned against them in Shanghai; thousands of Communists were arrested or killed within days, and the. urban underground organizations were nearly wiped out. It was at this critical juncture that Mao Zedong uttered his famous quote: "Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun. " On August 1st of the same year, with the Nanchang Uprising, the Communist Party formed its own army, which would later become the true core of the entire revolution. After being driven out of the cities, the Communist Party retreated to the countryside, building revolutionary base areas one by one in remote mountain regions. Truth be told, if the state apparatus of China at that time hadn't been so utterly rotten, the Communist Party would likely have disappeared from history long ago. The Nationalist government was financially weak, loosely disciplined, and constantly led by the nose by local. warlords who nominally obeyed the center but actually did as they pleased; Chiang Kai-shek was even kidnapped by his own allied warlords, and what truly pushed the Communist Party to the pinnacle of totalitarianism was the Long March. Under the encirclement of the Nationalists, the Red Army was forced into a long expedition, setting out from Jiangxi with over 80,000 people and arriving in the north a year later with only about 8,000 remaining. Yet, through this journey of death and starvation, they accomplished three things: they welded the core leadership into an ironclad unit, weeded out those with insufficient ability or wavering resolve , leaving behind the most capable and loyal group, and allowed Mao Zedong to.

secure supreme power. From this point on , the Communist Party grew into a highly cohesive party-army entity. On the Nationalist side, there were numerous factions and warlords suspicious of each other, where no one dared to turn their back on their own peers; whereas on the Communist side, the top leadership had climbed snowy mountains, gone hungry, and buried their comrades in the grasslands together. This kind of mutual trust is hard to quantify in any political textbook, but it became the regime's most important political asset for the next 40 years, and it would personally decide the fate of this regime at two life-or-death moments 40 years later. One was the Cultural Revolution, where Mao Zedong smashed the. entire state apparatus, yet the army did not seize power; the other was in 1989, when the order came down, and the army did not turn around to aim its guns at those who gave the command. However, victories on the battlefield alone could not build a totalitarian state. When the Communist Party entered Beijing, it still faced a China with extremely complex social relations. In rural areas , there were landlords, gentry, clans, temple fairs, and associations; in cities, there were capitalists, guilds, mission schools, secret societies, and various provincial and merchant chambers . These organizations were not necessarily anti-communist, and many were even neutral, yet each one served. as a power node independent of the Party . The most critical step in the CCP truly building a modern totalitarian state occurred in the seven years after 1949, not the moment they seized power; land reform was the first stroke, though many saw land reform only as "striking down local tyrants and distributing land ." Seeing only that the countryside had received land is merely looking at the surface. What was truly and thoroughly changed was the power structure that had persisted in rural China for thousands of years; a large group of new cadres from poor peasant backgrounds replaced the former gentry, representing the Party directly to manage villages, collect taxes, and adjudicate disputes. From then on, there was no longer a. political force in rural China independent of the central government; for the first time in Chinese history, the central regime could reach directly into every village in the country. With the outbreak of the Korean War in June 1950, it was as if an excuse for struggle had fallen from the sky. The CCP repackaged its domestic political purges as a war against imperialism to defend the homeland and the nation, claiming that the U.S., Nationalist remnants, and various counter-revolutionaries were colluding from within and without, making the purges faster, harsher, and more " justified." A series of movements— Suppression of Counter-revolutionaries, the Three-anti and Five-anti campaigns—. unfolded; those purged were far more than just Nationalist military and political personnel, but also included industrial and commercial owners, the gentry, religious groups, and secret societies—in short, all social forces that still retained the capacity for independent organization, a dimension that is rarely explained clearly. The CCP sought to eliminate far more than just specific entities; they intended to flatten the entire network of social organizational relations. This network had two layers: the first was the international network woven since the mid-19th century, which the CCP, in the name of anti-imperialism, confiscated entirely, closing or reforming mission.

schools, and expelling all missionaries and foreign residents, severing the private, commercial, religious, and academic ties between Chinese society and the outside world within a few years . The second layer was the domestic property network, where, under the banner of socialist public ownership and joint state-private enterprises, all private businesses were gradually incorporated and all private property rights were stripped away. By 1956, every Chinese person had become a proletarian in both name and reality. Your rice bowl, your housing, your food rations, and your children's education all relied on allocation; I still. remember visiting my hometown as a child and seeing that even their furniture had been assigned by the authorities—this was the forging of a party-state. What eventually took shape was an extremely rare totalitarian structure, a leadership core forged through the Long March, the Yan'an Rectification Movement , and the Civil War, bound by life-and-death ties. A highly politicized army whose true loyalty lies with the Party, rather than with the country or any constitution. And most crucially, the nationwide revolutionary movement essentially cleared out all alternative power centers that could. compete with it; urban entrepreneurs, intellectuals, foreign interests, rural landlords, clans, and religious organizations were either physically eliminated or completely marginalized. Filling this vacuum was the party-state apparatus, which reached into every capillary of the nation—neighborhood committees, work units, and people's communes gave the state the power to directly control population movement, food distribution, job assignments, and household registration, even managing what you said in meetings and wrote in your diary. It was this foundation that allowed the CCP, over the next 30 years. , to crawl out of one disaster after another that it had created with its own hands. By the 1960s, over a decade after the revolutionary victory, the passion for building a communist paradise began to ebb, and Mao grew restless, feeling that the revolutionary spirit was being slowly eroded by bureaucratization and institutionalization. Would this party become a mediocre ruling party that forgot its original intent and only wanted to coast along, or even become " KMT-ized"? At the same time, his own power was being bit by bit hollowed out by the massive bureaucratic system within the Party. It was amidst this anxiety that he launched the Cultural. Revolution, aiming to reshape the entire Chinese society, along with the Communist Party itself, through a bottom-up mass movement. He once said in 1966: "Great chaos leads to great order ." A dictator personally smashed the state machinery he had spent over a decade building, pushing the country to the brink of civil war, and the most bizarre thing is that even after doing this, the regime actually survived. The uniqueness of this crisis lies in the fact that the threat came entirely from within the system, having nothing to do with any external enemies. Mao Zedong incited the Red Guards to purge the top Party leadership, and within a few short years, party organizations from the central level down to the local level.

were paralyzed one after another. Large numbers of officials were purged and sent to "cow sheds," while major cities like Wuhan and Chongqing saw armed clashes involving heavy weaponry, bringing the country to the brink of civil war. At that time, the only state apparatus still functioning was the People's Liberation Army. How did it ultimately survive? The institutional legacy of the revolution remained, and the Party's authority was still deeply entrenched in every corner of society. Therefore, as long as Mao Zedong held the reins, local organizations could be rebuilt in a very short time. Decades of revolutionary struggle had long ago cleared away any potential organized. alternatives. Even with the country in chaos, no other force had the capacity to seize power. Most crucially, Mao always kept firm control over the PLA. In the end, it was the military that suppressed the factional fighting across the country. Those years were the most likely period for a military coup in modern Chinese history. The military held the guns, the civilian bureaucracy was almost entirely paralyzed, and the supreme leader was over 70. In 1971, Lin Biao, the officially designated successor whose name was written into the Party constitution, died in a plane crash following a failed coup attempt, yet the military never rose up. Even during the most chaotic moments, the. army remained steadfast in its support for the central leadership. The " Party-Army" unity forged during the revolutionary years proved its value for the second time. That second test came in 1989. The democracy movement was, in many ways, a byproduct of Deng Xiaoping’s reforms. Special economic zones, private enterprises, and rising living standards also brought severe inflation and official corruption. Along with increasingly loud calls for political reform. In the spring of 1989 , students took to the streets. Starting with mourning for reformist leader Hu Yaobang, it quickly evolved into demands for anti-corruption and democracy,. spreading to over 100 cities nationwide within a few weeks. There was heated debate within the Party over whether to use force. In the end, the decision was made by the revolutionary elders who had stepped behind the scenes but remained the ultimate decision-makers of the regime. The troops initially sent into the city were once blocked by Beijing citizens; at that moment, a true nationwide democratic movement seemed to be taking shape. This event was never just about a group of students trapped in a square. It was a nationwide movement involving workers, officials, soldiers, and even journalists—a protest followed by a crackdown. And what the. crackdown killed, beyond thousands of lives, was hope itself. A generation of optimistic young people was told overnight that a free life was something they could never count on. The central leadership ultimately suppressed the protests by relying on two familiar assets: the military did not experience a schism capable of challenging them, and the veterans, using their informal authority to command the military without needing formal titles, managed to bring the army into line. Unlike the Cultural Revolution, the 1989 protests failed from start to finish to develop an organization capable of mounting a full-scale confrontation with the regime . Though the numbers were large, there was no unified leadership, no clear agenda, and no capacity for long-term.

mobilization. Many participants did not belong to any political organization to begin with, making it very difficult to coalesce into a unified force. Looking back over these decades, you will find that the CCP has always relied on the same foundation to survive its crises. During the Great Famine, which killed tens of millions, not a single provincial party organization stood up to oppose it, because the land reform had long since cleared away all organized power in rural areas. During the Cultural Revolution, the entire bureaucratic system was smashed to pieces, yet the military never once considered seizing power; that army had been a part of the Party itself since its very inception. By 1989, when people. in over 100 cities took to the streets, the movement still couldn't coalesce. What truly mattered here was the total eradication of Chinese social organizational capacity by the revolution 40 years prior, which is why economic reform alone cannot explain this durability. Reform can make a regime stronger, wealthier, and better at management, but without the foundation laid by the revolution, the CCP would have struggled to survive the disasters it created time and time again . The revolution established the system , and the reform extended its lifespan. If you reverse this order, all your judgments about China are likely to be. incorrect. But at this point, a more troublesome problem begins to emerge. The logic of revolution can explain the period from 1949 to 1976, and even 1989 , but it cannot explain what happened after 2001. China joined the WTO, experienced 20 consecutive years of rapid economic growth, saw the rise of a new urban middle class numbering in the hundreds of millions, gained the world's largest population of netizens, and saw per capita GDP multiply more than tenfold. Following the precedents of South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Chile, this stage should have been the beginning of political liberalization. However, the result was the exact opposite: people in China today can say less than in the 1980s and read less. than in the 2010s. A society that has already modernized economically is moving backward politically. The revolutionary legacy cannot explain this ; it requires an entirely different set of explanations. In our next episode, we will answer this question, but before that, if you have any thoughts on what I just said, please feel free to leave them in the comments. Alright, that's all for today's show. Thank you for watching. Please click subscribe to the channel. I'm Gongzi Shen, and I'll see you in the next episode. Finally, a quick reminder that my new book, "The Truth About 'Insulting China': Misunderstandings Between China and the. World," has officially launched in Taiwan.

從清朝覆滅到軍閥割據，近代中國長期處於權力碎片化狀態，最終卻催生了史上最具韌性的威權體制之一。作者引用學術研究指出，由漫長且殘酷的社會革命所誕生的政權（如中、蘇、古巴、越南），往往對經濟危機、政策災難與外部制裁展現出極強的免疫力。這場革命留下了三項關鍵資產：以生死紐帶緊密結合的統治菁英階層、完全效忠該群體的暴力暴力專政機器，以及徹底被原子化、失去組織能力的社會。一般威權政權崩潰的三大途徑——菁英分裂、軍事政變與大眾起義，在早期暴力革命的淬鍊下已被完全封堵。

For a regime to reach this level, by any standard of political common sense, it should have been gone long ago. Yet, it never once collapsed; not only did it survive, but it also grew into the world's second-largest economy over the past few decades. The Soviet Union, its contemporary, collapsed; the socialist bloc in Eastern Europe, from Poland to Romania, fell like dominoes within two years. Even its neighbor across the strait, Taiwan, and. its neighbor to the northeast, South Korea, ended their authoritarian rule in the late 1980s and embraced liberal democracy. How has a regime that has committed every possible mistake survived until today? I know. many will say Deng Xiaoping's "Reform and Opening-up" saved the CCP. In 1911, the Qing Empire collapsed, and 2,000 years of imperial autocracy vanished overnight; over the next 30 years, warlords, secret societies, and local elites carved up the former Qing territories. From a chaotic, fragmented mess where factions constantly warred, one of the most enduring authoritarian regimes in modern history eventually emerged. This phenomenon demands an explanation, and the answer lies within the half-century-long Communist revolution. From 1925 to 1976, relying on Soviet support and successive waves of violent campaigns, the CCP forged a powerful, loyal force and a highly cohesive power core. This ultimately birthed the People's Republic of China, a party-state with integrated party, government, and military structures, clearing the way for decades of authoritarian rule. According to research from Harvard and the University of Toronto, if you compare regimes born from social revolutions—such as those in China, the USSR, Cuba, Iran, and Vietnam. —you find a common, exceptionally resilient trait: they are seemingly immune to economic crises, policy disasters, mass grievances, and external sanctions. What exactly is the reason for this? The reason lies in a revolutionary war that was sufficiently long and bloody, leaving them three precious legacies: a ruling elite bound by life-and-death ties, a violence-capable apparatus loyal solely to this group, and a hollowed-out, atomized society. Because all organizations capable of becoming competitors—churches, temples, military.

units, landed gentry, and chambers of commerce—were completely wiped out during the long process of so-called revolutionary struggle. Authoritarian regimes generally fall through only three paths: elite fragmentation, military coups, or mass uprisings; that Communist revolution happened to block all three. In the early 20th century, China was a tug-of-war between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party. They shared common enemies—imperialism, warlords, and local elites—all of which both parties verbally vowed to overthrow . However, when it came to the question of what kind of state to build, their. ideas were worlds apart. The Kuomintang's path was to integrate the existing warlords and have the landed gentry pledge loyalty to the Republic, trading the fastest unification for the lowest cost. This path looked smart, but the price was that those incorporated local forces never gave up their guns, their land, or their clan networks. Chiang Kai-shek unified China in name, but in reality, he held onto a group of partners who could turn against him at any moment. Mao Zedong and the Communist Party took a different path: they sought to eliminate the entire class of landlords who owned private property and. to uproot the warlords who defended local interests. The ultimate result of these nearly constant revolutionary movements was to force a nation with extremely fragmented power into a regime with highly centralized authority. For the first time in history, the so-called revolutionary struggle reached every village, every factory, every community , and even every household's dinner table in China. Initially, the Communist Party followed the Soviet model, pinning its hopes on the urban working class. That changed in April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek suddenly turned against them in Shanghai; thousands of Communists were arrested or killed within days, and the. urban underground organizations were nearly wiped out. It was at this critical juncture that Mao Zedong uttered his famous quote: "Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun. " On August 1st of the same year, with the Nanchang Uprising, the Communist Party formed its own army, which would later become the true core of the entire revolution. After being driven out of the cities, the Communist Party retreated to the countryside, building revolutionary base areas one by one in remote mountain regions. Truth be told, if the state apparatus of China at that time hadn't been so utterly rotten, the Communist Party would likely have disappeared from history long ago. The Nationalist government was financially weak, loosely disciplined, and constantly led by the nose by local. warlords who nominally obeyed the center but actually did as they pleased; Chiang Kai-shek was even kidnapped by his own allied warlords, and what truly pushed the Communist Party to the pinnacle of totalitarianism was the Long March. Under the encirclement of the Nationalists, the Red Army was forced into a long expedition, setting out from Jiangxi with over 80,000 people and arriving in the north a year later with only about 8,000 remaining. Yet, through this journey of death and starvation, they accomplished three things: they welded the core leadership into an ironclad unit, weeded out those with insufficient ability or wavering resolve , leaving behind the most capable and loyal group, and allowed Mao Zedong to.

secure supreme power. From this point on , the Communist Party grew into a highly cohesive party-army entity. On the Nationalist side, there were numerous factions and warlords suspicious of each other, where no one dared to turn their back on their own peers; whereas on the Communist side, the top leadership had climbed snowy mountains, gone hungry, and buried their comrades in the grasslands together. This kind of mutual trust is hard to quantify in any political textbook, but it became the regime's most important political asset for the next 40 years, and it would personally decide the fate of this regime at two life-or-death moments 40 years later. One was the Cultural Revolution, where Mao Zedong smashed the. entire state apparatus, yet the army did not seize power; the other was in 1989, when the order came down, and the army did not turn around to aim its guns at those who gave the command. However, victories on the battlefield alone could not build a totalitarian state. When the Communist Party entered Beijing, it still faced a China with extremely complex social relations. In rural areas , there were landlords, gentry, clans, temple fairs, and associations; in cities, there were capitalists, guilds, mission schools, secret societies, and various provincial and merchant chambers . These organizations were not necessarily anti-communist, and many were even neutral, yet each one served. as a power node independent of the Party . The most critical step in the CCP truly building a modern totalitarian state occurred in the seven years after 1949, not the moment they seized power; land reform was the first stroke, though many saw land reform only as "striking down local tyrants and distributing land ." Seeing only that the countryside had received land is merely looking at the surface. What was truly and thoroughly changed was the power structure that had persisted in rural China for thousands of years; a large group of new cadres from poor peasant backgrounds replaced the former gentry, representing the Party directly to manage villages, collect taxes, and adjudicate disputes. From then on, there was no longer a. political force in rural China independent of the central government; for the first time in Chinese history, the central regime could reach directly into every village in the country. With the outbreak of the Korean War in June 1950, it was as if an excuse for struggle had fallen from the sky. The CCP repackaged its domestic political purges as a war against imperialism to defend the homeland and the nation, claiming that the U.S., Nationalist remnants, and various counter-revolutionaries were colluding from within and without, making the purges faster, harsher, and more " justified." A series of movements— Suppression of Counter-revolutionaries, the Three-anti and Five-anti campaigns—. unfolded; those purged were far more than just Nationalist military and political personnel, but also included industrial and commercial owners, the gentry, religious groups, and secret societies—in short, all social forces that still retained the capacity for independent organization, a dimension that is rarely explained clearly. The CCP sought to eliminate far more than just specific entities; they intended to flatten the entire network of social organizational relations. This network had two layers: the first was the international network woven since the mid-19th century, which the CCP, in the name of anti-imperialism, confiscated entirely, closing or reforming mission.

schools, and expelling all missionaries and foreign residents, severing the private, commercial, religious, and academic ties between Chinese society and the outside world within a few years . The second layer was the domestic property network, where, under the banner of socialist public ownership and joint state-private enterprises, all private businesses were gradually incorporated and all private property rights were stripped away. By 1956, every Chinese person had become a proletarian in both name and reality. Your rice bowl, your housing, your food rations, and your children's education all relied on allocation; I still. remember visiting my hometown as a child and seeing that even their furniture had been assigned by the authorities—this was the forging of a party-state. What eventually took shape was an extremely rare totalitarian structure, a leadership core forged through the Long March, the Yan'an Rectification Movement , and the Civil War, bound by life-and-death ties. A highly politicized army whose true loyalty lies with the Party, rather than with the country or any constitution. And most crucially, the nationwide revolutionary movement essentially cleared out all alternative power centers that could. compete with it; urban entrepreneurs, intellectuals, foreign interests, rural landlords, clans, and religious organizations were either physically eliminated or completely marginalized. Filling this vacuum was the party-state apparatus, which reached into every capillary of the nation—neighborhood committees, work units, and people's communes gave the state the power to directly control population movement, food distribution, job assignments, and household registration, even managing what you said in meetings and wrote in your diary. It was this foundation that allowed the CCP, over the next 30 years. , to crawl out of one disaster after another that it had created with its own hands. By the 1960s, over a decade after the revolutionary victory, the passion for building a communist paradise began to ebb, and Mao grew restless, feeling that the revolutionary spirit was being slowly eroded by bureaucratization and institutionalization. Would this party become a mediocre ruling party that forgot its original intent and only wanted to coast along, or even become " KMT-ized"? At the same time, his own power was being bit by bit hollowed out by the massive bureaucratic system within the Party. It was amidst this anxiety that he launched the Cultural. Revolution, aiming to reshape the entire Chinese society, along with the Communist Party itself, through a bottom-up mass movement. He once said in 1966: "Great chaos leads to great order ." A dictator personally smashed the state machinery he had spent over a decade building, pushing the country to the brink of civil war, and the most bizarre thing is that even after doing this, the regime actually survived. The uniqueness of this crisis lies in the fact that the threat came entirely from within the system, having nothing to do with any external enemies. Mao Zedong incited the Red Guards to purge the top Party leadership, and within a few short years, party organizations from the central level down to the local level.

were paralyzed one after another. Large numbers of officials were purged and sent to "cow sheds," while major cities like Wuhan and Chongqing saw armed clashes involving heavy weaponry, bringing the country to the brink of civil war. At that time, the only state apparatus still functioning was the People's Liberation Army. How did it ultimately survive? The institutional legacy of the revolution remained, and the Party's authority was still deeply entrenched in every corner of society. Therefore, as long as Mao Zedong held the reins, local organizations could be rebuilt in a very short time. Decades of revolutionary struggle had long ago cleared away any potential organized. alternatives. Even with the country in chaos, no other force had the capacity to seize power. Most crucially, Mao always kept firm control over the PLA. In the end, it was the military that suppressed the factional fighting across the country. Those years were the most likely period for a military coup in modern Chinese history. The military held the guns, the civilian bureaucracy was almost entirely paralyzed, and the supreme leader was over 70. In 1971, Lin Biao, the officially designated successor whose name was written into the Party constitution, died in a plane crash following a failed coup attempt, yet the military never rose up. Even during the most chaotic moments, the. army remained steadfast in its support for the central leadership. The " Party-Army" unity forged during the revolutionary years proved its value for the second time. That second test came in 1989. The democracy movement was, in many ways, a byproduct of Deng Xiaoping’s reforms. Special economic zones, private enterprises, and rising living standards also brought severe inflation and official corruption. Along with increasingly loud calls for political reform. In the spring of 1989 , students took to the streets. Starting with mourning for reformist leader Hu Yaobang, it quickly evolved into demands for anti-corruption and democracy,. spreading to over 100 cities nationwide within a few weeks. There was heated debate within the Party over whether to use force. In the end, the decision was made by the revolutionary elders who had stepped behind the scenes but remained the ultimate decision-makers of the regime. The troops initially sent into the city were once blocked by Beijing citizens; at that moment, a true nationwide democratic movement seemed to be taking shape. This event was never just about a group of students trapped in a square. It was a nationwide movement involving workers, officials, soldiers, and even journalists—a protest followed by a crackdown. And what the. crackdown killed, beyond thousands of lives, was hope itself. A generation of optimistic young people was told overnight that a free life was something they could never count on. The central leadership ultimately suppressed the protests by relying on two familiar assets: the military did not experience a schism capable of challenging them, and the veterans, using their informal authority to command the military without needing formal titles, managed to bring the army into line. Unlike the Cultural Revolution, the 1989 protests failed from start to finish to develop an organization capable of mounting a full-scale confrontation with the regime . Though the numbers were large, there was no unified leadership, no clear agenda, and no capacity for long-term.

mobilization. Many participants did not belong to any political organization to begin with, making it very difficult to coalesce into a unified force. Looking back over these decades, you will find that the CCP has always relied on the same foundation to survive its crises. During the Great Famine, which killed tens of millions, not a single provincial party organization stood up to oppose it, because the land reform had long since cleared away all organized power in rural areas. During the Cultural Revolution, the entire bureaucratic system was smashed to pieces, yet the military never once considered seizing power; that army had been a part of the Party itself since its very inception. By 1989, when people. in over 100 cities took to the streets, the movement still couldn't coalesce. What truly mattered here was the total eradication of Chinese social organizational capacity by the revolution 40 years prior, which is why economic reform alone cannot explain this durability. Reform can make a regime stronger, wealthier, and better at management, but without the foundation laid by the revolution, the CCP would have struggled to survive the disasters it created time and time again . The revolution established the system , and the reform extended its lifespan. If you reverse this order, all your judgments about China are likely to be. incorrect. But at this point, a more troublesome problem begins to emerge. The logic of revolution can explain the period from 1949 to 1976, and even 1989 , but it cannot explain what happened after 2001. China joined the WTO, experienced 20 consecutive years of rapid economic growth, saw the rise of a new urban middle class numbering in the hundreds of millions, gained the world's largest population of netizens, and saw per capita GDP multiply more than tenfold. Following the precedents of South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Chile, this stage should have been the beginning of political liberalization. However, the result was the exact opposite: people in China today can say less than in the 1980s and read less. than in the 2010s. A society that has already modernized economically is moving backward politically. The revolutionary legacy cannot explain this ; it requires an entirely different set of explanations. In our next episode, we will answer this question, but before that, if you have any thoughts on what I just said, please feel free to leave them in the comments. Alright, that's all for today's show. Thank you for watching. Please click subscribe to the channel. I'm Gongzi Shen, and I'll see you in the next episode. Finally, a quick reminder that my new book, "The Truth About 'Insulting China': Misunderstandings Between China and the. World," has officially launched in Taiwan.

從清朝覆滅到軍閥割據，近代中國長期處於權力碎片化狀態，最終卻催生了史上最具韌性的威權體制之一。作者引用學術研究指出，由漫長且殘酷的社會革命所誕生的政權（如中、蘇、古巴、越南），往往對經濟危機、政策災難與外部制裁展現出極強的免疫力。這場革命留下了三項關鍵資產：以生死紐帶緊密結合的統治菁英階層、完全效忠該群體的暴力暴力專政機器，以及徹底被原子化、失去組織能力的社會。一般威權政權崩潰的三大途徑——菁英分裂、軍事政變與大眾起義，在早期暴力革命的淬鍊下已被完全封堵。

國共建國路徑之別與極權組織的成型

相較於國民黨採取懷柔與收編軍閥、鄉紳以求快速統戰，卻留下各自為政的後患；中共選擇以暴力手段徹底剷除地主階級與地方軍閥，將權力徹底滲透至農村、工廠與家庭餐桌。歷經1927年清黨的重創後，毛澤東確立了「槍桿子裡面出政權」的原則，打造了黨軍一體的架構。隨後的長征更成為極權體制凝聚的轉捩點，在經歷殘酷淘汰後，留下了極為精簡且忠誠的領導核心，不僅確立了毛澤東的絕對權力，更鍛造出國民黨派系所無法比擬的深厚信任與高度凝聚力，成為日後政權維繫數十年的最核心政治資產。

================================================

Ten years after this regime starved tens of millions of its own people, it pushed the country to the brink of full-scale civil war, and twenty years after that, it opened fire on its own people in its own capital. For a regime to reach this level, by any standard of political common sense, it should have been gone long ago. Yet, it never once collapsed; not only did it survive, but it also grew into the world's second-largest economy over the past few decades. The Soviet Union, its contemporary, collapsed; the socialist bloc in Eastern Europe, from Poland to Romania, fell like dominoes within two years. Even its neighbor across the strait, Taiwan, and. its neighbor to the northeast, South Korea, ended their authoritarian rule in the late 1980s and embraced liberal democracy. Yet, the one-party Chinese Communist Party has remained in power in China to this day. I have produced many episodes arguing that the CCP's rule has entered a countdown. Today, I want to answer a different question—a harder one that few are willing to answer seriously : Why didn't this countdown happen in 1960, 1976, or 1989? How has a regime that has committed every possible mistake survived until today? I know. many will say Deng Xiaoping's "Reform and Opening-up" saved the CCP. This has been the prevailing view in Western academia and politics for the past 40 years: economic growth bought social stability, and the CCP stayed stable because it knew how to adapt and was lucky enough to catch the global takeoff of the 80s and 90s. The scale of China’s economic transformation is indeed astonishing—no one can deny that—but by focusing only on these last 40 years, you miss an earlier and more important precondition: When Deng issued his order in 1978, he was able to overturn the entire line of class struggle that Mao. had pursued for decades. How was he able to do that? There was no organized resistance across the country, no provincial secession, no military mutiny , and no political faction stood up to say no. How could he achieve this? The answer is that before he issued his order, someone had already built this country for him. A machine that would turn as a whole as soon as Zhongnanhai flipped the switch. The Reform and Opening-up was the result of this machine starting, but it was not the beginning of the story. Hello everyone, at the beginning of this episode, I’d like to take a moment to share a few personal thoughts. I’ve been making. these programs for seven years now, with over 2,000 episodes, and many viewers often ask: How do you acquire knowledge and information, and how do you analyze and judge them? So, the answer is finally revealed today in my latest book , "The Truth About 'Ru-Hua': Misunderstandings Between China and the World Order." This book covers everything from China's ancient and modern history to the history of the PRC , cross-strait issues, international relations, America's role in this order , and the underlying logic behind these current events. I believe this book is a massive resource for my friends in Taiwan and across the globe who embrace universal values and aim to be global citizens—it is a weapon for.

understanding the world and confronting authoritarianism. I consider this very important; it is the culmination of my work over the years, detailing my sources of knowledge, my analytical frameworks, and the process by which I reach my conclusions. It presents all of that, as many who have watched my " Gongzi Reads" series—which is currently on hiatus on my channel—can attest. All the content from that series is in this book, along with many new, even more significant theories and facts. Of course, I am standing on the shoulders of giants, utilizing a wealth of geopolitical and international relations. theories to enrich this book, providing better tools to understand world changes and our place in it, so we can live more harmoniously with this world. I hope you enjoy the book; it is now officially available for order on Books.com.tw in Taiwan. For those outside of Taiwan and its surrounding regions, such as in North America or Europe, I will announce other channels for purchase soon. Also, if you buy the book and would like it signed, there will be a book signing event in Taipei on December 5th; everyone is welcome, and I will post the time and address on my YouTube channel. Thank you, and now back to the main. topic. >> So first, we must return to history to find the answers. In 1911, the Qing Empire collapsed, and 2,000 years of imperial autocracy vanished overnight; over the next 30 years, warlords, secret societies, and local elites carved up the former Qing territories. From a chaotic, fragmented mess where factions constantly warred, one of the most enduring authoritarian regimes in modern history eventually emerged. This phenomenon demands an explanation, and the answer lies within the half-century-long Communist revolution. From 1925 to 1976, relying on Soviet support and successive waves of violent campaigns, the CCP forged a powerful, loyal force and a highly cohesive power core. This ultimately birthed the People's Republic of China, a party-state with integrated party, government, and military structures, clearing the way for decades of authoritarian rule. According to research from Harvard and the University of Toronto, if you compare regimes born from social revolutions—such as those in China, the USSR, Cuba, Iran, and Vietnam. —you find a common, exceptionally resilient trait: they are seemingly immune to economic crises, policy disasters, mass grievances, and external sanctions. What exactly is the reason for this? The reason lies in a revolutionary war that was sufficiently long and bloody, leaving them three precious legacies: a ruling elite bound by life-and-death ties, a violence-capable apparatus loyal solely to this group, and a hollowed-out, atomized society. Because all organizations capable of becoming competitors—churches, temples, military.

units, landed gentry, and chambers of commerce—were completely wiped out during the long process of so-called revolutionary struggle. Authoritarian regimes generally fall through only three paths: elite fragmentation, military coups, or mass uprisings; that Communist revolution happened to block all three. In the early 20th century, China was a tug-of-war between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party. They shared common enemies—imperialism, warlords, and local elites—all of which both parties verbally vowed to overthrow . However, when it came to the question of what kind of state to build, their. ideas were worlds apart. The Kuomintang's path was to integrate the existing warlords and have the landed gentry pledge loyalty to the Republic, trading the fastest unification for the lowest cost. This path looked smart, but the price was that those incorporated local forces never gave up their guns, their land, or their clan networks. Chiang Kai-shek unified China in name, but in reality, he held onto a group of partners who could turn against him at any moment. Mao Zedong and the Communist Party took a different path: they sought to eliminate the entire class of landlords who owned private property and. to uproot the warlords who defended local interests. The ultimate result of these nearly constant revolutionary movements was to force a nation with extremely fragmented power into a regime with highly centralized authority. For the first time in history, the so-called revolutionary struggle reached every village, every factory, every community , and even every household's dinner table in China. Initially, the Communist Party followed the Soviet model, pinning its hopes on the urban working class. That changed in April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek suddenly turned against them in Shanghai; thousands of Communists were arrested or killed within days, and the. urban underground organizations were nearly wiped out. It was at this critical juncture that Mao Zedong uttered his famous quote: "Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun. " On August 1st of the same year, with the Nanchang Uprising, the Communist Party formed its own army, which would later become the true core of the entire revolution. After being driven out of the cities, the Communist Party retreated to the countryside, building revolutionary base areas one by one in remote mountain regions. Truth be told, if the state apparatus of China at that time hadn't been so utterly rotten, the Communist Party would likely have disappeared from history long ago. The Nationalist government was financially weak, loosely disciplined, and constantly led by the nose by local. warlords who nominally obeyed the center but actually did as they pleased; Chiang Kai-shek was even kidnapped by his own allied warlords, and what truly pushed the Communist Party to the pinnacle of totalitarianism was the Long March. Under the encirclement of the Nationalists, the Red Army was forced into a long expedition, setting out from Jiangxi with over 80,000 people and arriving in the north a year later with only about 8,000 remaining. Yet, through this journey of death and starvation, they accomplished three things: they welded the core leadership into an ironclad unit, weeded out those with insufficient ability or wavering resolve , leaving behind the most capable and loyal group, and allowed Mao Zedong to.

secure supreme power. From this point on , the Communist Party grew into a highly cohesive party-army entity. On the Nationalist side, there were numerous factions and warlords suspicious of each other, where no one dared to turn their back on their own peers; whereas on the Communist side, the top leadership had climbed snowy mountains, gone hungry, and buried their comrades in the grasslands together. This kind of mutual trust is hard to quantify in any political textbook, but it became the regime's most important political asset for the next 40 years, and it would personally decide the fate of this regime at two life-or-death moments 40 years later. One was the Cultural Revolution, where Mao Zedong smashed the. entire state apparatus, yet the army did not seize power; the other was in 1989, when the order came down, and the army did not turn around to aim its guns at those who gave the command. However, victories on the battlefield alone could not build a totalitarian state. When the Communist Party entered Beijing, it still faced a China with extremely complex social relations. In rural areas , there were landlords, gentry, clans, temple fairs, and associations; in cities, there were capitalists, guilds, mission schools, secret societies, and various provincial and merchant chambers . These organizations were not necessarily anti-communist, and many were even neutral, yet each one served. as a power node independent of the Party . The most critical step in the CCP truly building a modern totalitarian state occurred in the seven years after 1949, not the moment they seized power; land reform was the first stroke, though many saw land reform only as "striking down local tyrants and distributing land ." Seeing only that the countryside had received land is merely looking at the surface. What was truly and thoroughly changed was the power structure that had persisted in rural China for thousands of years; a large group of new cadres from poor peasant backgrounds replaced the former gentry, representing the Party directly to manage villages, collect taxes, and adjudicate disputes. From then on, there was no longer a. political force in rural China independent of the central government; for the first time in Chinese history, the central regime could reach directly into every village in the country. With the outbreak of the Korean War in June 1950, it was as if an excuse for struggle had fallen from the sky. The CCP repackaged its domestic political purges as a war against imperialism to defend the homeland and the nation, claiming that the U.S., Nationalist remnants, and various counter-revolutionaries were colluding from within and without, making the purges faster, harsher, and more " justified." A series of movements— Suppression of Counter-revolutionaries, the Three-anti and Five-anti campaigns—. unfolded; those purged were far more than just Nationalist military and political personnel, but also included industrial and commercial owners, the gentry, religious groups, and secret societies—in short, all social forces that still retained the capacity for independent organization, a dimension that is rarely explained clearly. The CCP sought to eliminate far more than just specific entities; they intended to flatten the entire network of social organizational relations. This network had two layers: the first was the international network woven since the mid-19th century, which the CCP, in the name of anti-imperialism, confiscated entirely, closing or reforming mission.

schools, and expelling all missionaries and foreign residents, severing the private, commercial, religious, and academic ties between Chinese society and the outside world within a few years . The second layer was the domestic property network, where, under the banner of socialist public ownership and joint state-private enterprises, all private businesses were gradually incorporated and all private property rights were stripped away. By 1956, every Chinese person had become a proletarian in both name and reality. Your rice bowl, your housing, your food rations, and your children's education all relied on allocation; I still. remember visiting my hometown as a child and seeing that even their furniture had been assigned by the authorities—this was the forging of a party-state. What eventually took shape was an extremely rare totalitarian structure, a leadership core forged through the Long March, the Yan'an Rectification Movement , and the Civil War, bound by life-and-death ties. A highly politicized army whose true loyalty lies with the Party, rather than with the country or any constitution. And most crucially, the nationwide revolutionary movement essentially cleared out all alternative power centers that could. compete with it; urban entrepreneurs, intellectuals, foreign interests, rural landlords, clans, and religious organizations were either physically eliminated or completely marginalized. Filling this vacuum was the party-state apparatus, which reached into every capillary of the nation—neighborhood committees, work units, and people's communes gave the state the power to directly control population movement, food distribution, job assignments, and household registration, even managing what you said in meetings and wrote in your diary. It was this foundation that allowed the CCP, over the next 30 years. , to crawl out of one disaster after another that it had created with its own hands. By the 1960s, over a decade after the revolutionary victory, the passion for building a communist paradise began to ebb, and Mao grew restless, feeling that the revolutionary spirit was being slowly eroded by bureaucratization and institutionalization. Would this party become a mediocre ruling party that forgot its original intent and only wanted to coast along, or even become " KMT-ized"? At the same time, his own power was being bit by bit hollowed out by the massive bureaucratic system within the Party. It was amidst this anxiety that he launched the Cultural. Revolution, aiming to reshape the entire Chinese society, along with the Communist Party itself, through a bottom-up mass movement. He once said in 1966: "Great chaos leads to great order ." A dictator personally smashed the state machinery he had spent over a decade building, pushing the country to the brink of civil war, and the most bizarre thing is that even after doing this, the regime actually survived. The uniqueness of this crisis lies in the fact that the threat came entirely from within the system, having nothing to do with any external enemies. Mao Zedong incited the Red Guards to purge the top Party leadership, and within a few short years, party organizations from the central level down to the local level.

were paralyzed one after another. Large numbers of officials were purged and sent to "cow sheds," while major cities like Wuhan and Chongqing saw armed clashes involving heavy weaponry, bringing the country to the brink of civil war. At that time, the only state apparatus still functioning was the People's Liberation Army. How did it ultimately survive? The institutional legacy of the revolution remained, and the Party's authority was still deeply entrenched in every corner of society. Therefore, as long as Mao Zedong held the reins, local organizations could be rebuilt in a very short time. Decades of revolutionary struggle had long ago cleared away any potential organized. alternatives. Even with the country in chaos, no other force had the capacity to seize power. Most crucially, Mao always kept firm control over the PLA. In the end, it was the military that suppressed the factional fighting across the country. Those years were the most likely period for a military coup in modern Chinese history. The military held the guns, the civilian bureaucracy was almost entirely paralyzed, and the supreme leader was over 70. In 1971, Lin Biao, the officially designated successor whose name was written into the Party constitution, died in a plane crash following a failed coup attempt, yet the military never rose up. Even during the most chaotic moments, the. army remained steadfast in its support for the central leadership. The " Party-Army" unity forged during the revolutionary years proved its value for the second time. That second test came in 1989. The democracy movement was, in many ways, a byproduct of Deng Xiaoping’s reforms. Special economic zones, private enterprises, and rising living standards also brought severe inflation and official corruption. Along with increasingly loud calls for political reform. In the spring of 1989 , students took to the streets. Starting with mourning for reformist leader Hu Yaobang, it quickly evolved into demands for anti-corruption and democracy,. spreading to over 100 cities nationwide within a few weeks. There was heated debate within the Party over whether to use force. In the end, the decision was made by the revolutionary elders who had stepped behind the scenes but remained the ultimate decision-makers of the regime. The troops initially sent into the city were once blocked by Beijing citizens; at that moment, a true nationwide democratic movement seemed to be taking shape. This event was never just about a group of students trapped in a square. It was a nationwide movement involving workers, officials, soldiers, and even journalists—a protest followed by a crackdown. And what the. crackdown killed, beyond thousands of lives, was hope itself. A generation of optimistic young people was told overnight that a free life was something they could never count on. The central leadership ultimately suppressed the protests by relying on two familiar assets: the military did not experience a schism capable of challenging them, and the veterans, using their informal authority to command the military without needing formal titles, managed to bring the army into line. Unlike the Cultural Revolution, the 1989 protests failed from start to finish to develop an organization capable of mounting a full-scale confrontation with the regime . Though the numbers were large, there was no unified leadership, no clear agenda, and no capacity for long-term.

mobilization. Many participants did not belong to any political organization to begin with, making it very difficult to coalesce into a unified force. Looking back over these decades, you will find that the CCP has always relied on the same foundation to survive its crises. During the Great Famine, which killed tens of millions, not a single provincial party organization stood up to oppose it, because the land reform had long since cleared away all organized power in rural areas. During the Cultural Revolution, the entire bureaucratic system was smashed to pieces, yet the military never once considered seizing power; that army had been a part of the Party itself since its very inception. By 1989, when people. in over 100 cities took to the streets, the movement still couldn't coalesce. What truly mattered here was the total eradication of Chinese social organizational capacity by the revolution 40 years prior, which is why economic reform alone cannot explain this durability. Reform can make a regime stronger, wealthier, and better at management, but without the foundation laid by the revolution, the CCP would have struggled to survive the disasters it created time and time again . The revolution established the system , and the reform extended its lifespan. If you reverse this order, all your judgments about China are likely to be. incorrect. But at this point, a more troublesome problem begins to emerge. The logic of revolution can explain the period from 1949 to 1976, and even 1989 , but it cannot explain what happened after 2001. China joined the WTO, experienced 20 consecutive years of rapid economic growth, saw the rise of a new urban middle class numbering in the hundreds of millions, gained the world's largest population of netizens, and saw per capita GDP multiply more than tenfold. Following the precedents of South Korea, Taiwan, Spain, and Chile, this stage should have been the beginning of political liberalization. However, the result was the exact opposite: people in China today can say less than in the 1980s and read less. than in the 2010s. A society that has already modernized economically is moving backward politically. The revolutionary legacy cannot explain this ; it requires an entirely different set of explanations. In our next episode, we will answer this question, but before that, if you have any thoughts on what I just said, please feel free to leave them in the comments. Alright, that's all for today's show. Thank you for watching. Please click subscribe to the channel. I'm Gongzi Shen, and I'll see you in the next episode. Finally, a quick reminder that my new book, "The Truth About 'Insulting China': Misunderstandings Between China and the. World," has officially launched in Taiwan.

  • 整理作者對「中華人民共和國」國名與政治體制的批判，呈現其對「中華」、「人民」及「共和」三個概念的重新檢視。

摘要

新書主旨與秦漢政治傳統

作者介紹新書《辱華的真相：被誤解的中國和世界秩序》，並說明書名中的「辱華」一詞，反映中國政府常將不同立場或批評貼上反華標籤。作者進一步質疑「中華人民共和國」的國名與實際政治狀態，認為其既不真正代表中華文明，也不代表人民，更不是共和國。

作者將中國長期的政治運作概括為「秦漢政體」：表面尊崇儒家，實際依靠法家式的中央集權。作者認為，秦始皇建立的大一統秩序壓縮了地方自治、對外交流與思想競爭，並使政治反覆陷入集權、腐敗、崩潰，再度統一的循環。他也指出，先秦與兩宋等中央控制相對較弱的時期，曾展現出更繁盛的文明面貌。

談到近代民族認同時，作者認為「中華民族」是清末因政治需要而建構的概念，將原有帝國重新包裝成民族國家。他回顧1920年代的聯省自治運動，認為大一統觀念曾阻礙地方自治的發展；並指出中共早期受到共產國際及蘇聯共產黨扶植，其體制結合了列寧主義與中國傳統的集權統治。作者也反駁以「劣根性」解釋社會習性，認為相關現象更應從長期專制環境理解。

黨國體制、人民與共和

作者以「完美的獨裁」形容中共政權，認為其控制深入日常生活，使部分民眾真心支持，而反對聲音則可能遭到壓制。他指出，黨國體制的首要目標是維持自身存續，並將百年屈辱、毛澤東以暴力奪權，以及蘇聯解體視為影響中共決策的重要歷史記憶。作者也提到，延安整風時期已可見內部清洗與集權的模式，後來這套治理方式擴展至全國。
